source_text:
Μακρόθυμος, φησί, γίνου καὶ συνετός, καὶ πάντων τῶν πονηρῶν ἔργων κατακυριεύσεις καὶ ἐργάσῃ πᾶσαν δικαιοσύνην.
ἐὰν γὰρ μακρόθυμος ἔσῃ, τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον τὸ κατοικοῦν ἐν σοὶ καθαρὸν ἔσται, μὴ ἐπισκοτούμενον ὑπὸ ἑτέρου πονηροῦ πνεύματος, ἀλλ’ ἐν εὐρυχώρῳ κατοικοῦν ἀγαλλιάσεται καὶ εὐφρανθήσεται μετὰ τοῦ σκεύους, ἐν ᾧ κατοικεῖ, καὶ λειτουργήσει τῷ θεῷ ἐν ἱλαρότητι πολλῇ, ἔχον τὴν εὐθηνίαν ἐν ἑαυτῷ.
ἐὰν δὲ ὀξυχολία τις προσέλθῃ, εὐθὺς τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον, τρυφερὸν ὄν, στενοχωρεῖται, μὴ ἔχον τὸν τόπον καθαρόν, καὶ ζητεῖ ἀποστῆναι ἐκ τοῦ τόπου: πνίγεται γὰρ ὑπὸ τοῦ πονηροῦ πνεύματος, μὴ ἔχον τόπον λειτουργῆσαι τῷ κυρίῳ, καθὼς βούλεται, μιαινόμενον ὑπὸ τῆς ὀξυχολίας. ἐν γὰρ τῇ μακροθυμίᾳ ὁ κύριος κατοικεῖ, ἐν δὲ τῇ ὀξυχολίᾳ ὁ διάβολος.
ἀμφότερα οὖν τὰ πνεύματα ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ κατοικοῦντα, ἀσύμφορόν ἐστιν καὶ πονηρὸν τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ ἐκείνῳ, ἐν ᾧ κατοικοῦσιν.
ἐὰν γὰρ λάβῃς ἀψινθίου μικρὸν λίαν καὶ εἰς κεράμιον μέλιτος ἐπιχέῃς, οὐχὶ ὅλον τὸ μέλι ἀφανίζεται, καὶ τοσοῦτον μέλι ὑπὸ τοῦ ἐλαχίστου ἀψινθίου ἀπόλλυται καὶ ἀπόλλυσι τὴν γλυκύτητα τοῦ μέλιτος, καὶ οὐκέτι τὴν αὐτὴν χάριν ἔχει παρὰ τῷ δεσπότῃ, ὅτι ἐπικράνθη καὶ τὴν χρῆσιν αὐτοῦ ἀπώλεσεν; ἐὰν δὲ εἰς τὸ μέλι μὴ βληθῇ τὸ ἀψίνθιον, γλυκὺ εὑρίσκεται τὸ μέλι καὶ εὔχρηστον γίνεται τῷ δεσπότῃ αὐτοῦ.
βλέπεις ὅτι ἡ μακροθυμία γλυκυτάτη ἐστὶν ὑπὲρ τὸ μέλι καὶ εὔχρηστός ἐστι τῷ κυρίῳ, καὶ ἐν αὐτῇ κατοικεῖ. ἡ δὲ ὀξυχολία πικρὰ καὶ ἄχρηστός ἐστιν. ἐὰν οὖν μιγῇ ἡ ὀξυχολία τῇ μακροθυμίᾳ, μιαίνεται ἡ μακροθυμία καὶ οὐκέτι εὔχρηστός ἐστι τῷ θεῷ ἡ ἔντευξις αὐτῆς.
Ἤθελον, φημί, κύριε, γνῶναι τὴν ἐνέργειαν τῆς ὀξυχολίας, ἵνα φυλάξωμαι ἀπ’ αὐτῆς. Καὶ μήν, φησίν, ἐὰν μὴ φυλάξῃ ἀπ’ αὐτῆς σὺ καὶ ὁ οἶκός σου, ἀπώλεσάς σου τὴν πᾶσαν ἐλπίδα. ἀλλὰ φύλαξαι ἀπ’ αὐτῆς: ἐγὼ γὰρ μετὰ σοῦ εἰμί. καὶ πάντες δὲ ἀφέξονται ἀπ’ αὐτῆς, ὅσοι ἂν μετανοήσωσιν ἐξ ὅλης τῆς καρδίας αὐτῶν: μετ’ αὐτῶν γὰρ ἔσομαι καὶ συντηρήσω αὐτούς: ἐδικαιώθησαν γὰρ πάντες ὑπὸ τοῦ σεμνοτάτου ἀγγέλου.
Ἄκουε νῦν, φησί, τὴν ἐνέργειαν τῆς ὀξυχολίας, πῶς πονηρά ἐστι, καὶ πῶς τοὺς δούλους μοῦ καταστρέφει τῇ ἑαυτῆς ἐνεργείᾳ καὶ πῶς ἀποπλανᾷ αὐτοὺς ἀπὸ τῆς δικαιοσύνης. οὐκ ἀποπλανᾷ δὲ τοὺς πλήρεις ὄντας ἐν τῇ πίστει οὐδὲ ἐνεργῆσαι δύναται εἰς αὐτούς, ὅτι ἡ δύναμις μου μετ’ αὐτῶν ἐστιν: ἀποπλανᾷ δὲ τοὺς ἀποκένους καὶ διψύχους ὄντας.
ὅταν δὲ ἴδῃ τοὺς τοιούτους ἀνθρώπους εὐσταθοῦντας, παρεμβάλλει ἑαυτὴν εἰς τὴν καρδίαν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐκείνου, καὶ ἐκ τοῦ μηδενὸς ὁ ἀνὴρ ἢ ἡ γυνὴ ἐν πικρίᾳ γίνεται ἕνεκεν βιωτικῶν πραγμάτων ἢ περὶ ἐδεσμάτων ἢ μικρολογίας τινὸς ἢ περὶ φίλου τινὸς ἢ περὶ δόσεως ἢ λήψεως ἢ περὶ τοιούτων μωρῶν πραγμάτων: ταῦτα γὰρ πάντα μωρά ἐστι καὶ κενὰ καὶ ἄφρονα καὶ ἀσύμφορα τοῖς δούλοις τοῦ θεοῦ.
ἡ δὲ μακροθυμία μεγάλη ἐστὶ καὶ ἰσχυρὰ καὶ δύναμιν ἔχουσα καὶ στιβαρὰν καὶ εὐθηνουμένην ἐν πλατυσμῷ μεγάλῳ, ἱλαρά, ἀγαλλιωμένη, ἀμέριμνος οὖσα, δοξάζουσα τὸν κύριον ἐν παντὶ καιρῷ, μηδὲν ἐν ἑαυτῇ ἔχουσα πικρόν, παραμένουσα διὰ παντὸς πραεῖα καὶ ἡσύχιος: αὕτη οὖν ἡ μακροθυμία κατοικεῖ μετὰ τῶν τὴν πίστιν ἐχόντων ὁλόκληρον.
ἡ δὲ ὀξυχολία πρῶτον μὲν μωρά ἐστιν, ἐλαφρά τε καὶ ἄφρων. εἶτα ἐκ τῆς ἀφροσύνης γίνεται πικρία, ἐκ δὲ τῆς πικρίας θυμός, ἐκ δὲ τοῦ θυμοῦ ὀργή, ἐκ δὲ τῆς ὀργῆς μῆνις: εἶτα ἡ μῆνις αὕτη ἐκ τοσούτων κακῶν συνισταμένη γίνεται ἁμαρτία μεγάλη καὶ ἀνίατος.
ὅταν γὰρ ταῦτα τὰ πνεύματα ἐν ἑνὶ ἀγγείῳ κατοικῇ, οὗ καὶ τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον κατοικεῖ, οὐ χωρεῖ τὸ ἄγγος ἐκεῖνο, ἀλλ’ ὑπερπλεονάζει.
τὸ τρυφερὸν οὖν πνεῦμα, μὴ ἔχον συνήθειαν μετὰ πονηροῦ πνεύματος κατοικεῖν μηδὲ μετὰ σκληρότητος, ἀποχωρεῖ ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου τοῦ τοιούτου καὶ ζητεῖ κατοικεῖν μετὰ πραότητος καὶ ἡσυχίας.
εἶτα ὅταν ἀποστῇ ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐκείνου, οὗ κατοικεῖ, γίνεται ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἐκεῖνος κενὸς ἀπὸ τοῦ πνεύματος τοῦ δικαίου, καὶ τὸ λοιπὸν πεπληρωμένος τοῖς πνεύμασι τοῖς πονηροῖς ἀκαταστατεῖ ἐν πάσῃ πράξει αὐτοῦ, περισπώμενος ὧδε κἀκεῖσε ἀπὸ τῶν πνευμάτων τῶν πονηρῶν, καὶ ὅλως ἀποτυφλοῦται ἀπὸ τῆς διανοίας τῆς ἀγαθῆς. οὕτως οὖν συμβαίνει πᾶσι τοῖς ὀξυχόλοις.
ἀπέχου οὖν ἀπὸ τῆς ὀξυχολίας, τοῦ πονηροτάτου πνεύματος: ἔνδυσαι δὲ τὴν μακροθυμίαν καὶ ἀντίστα τῇ ὀξυχολίᾳ καὶ τῇ πικρίᾳ, καὶ ἔσῃ εὑρισκόμενος μετὰ τῆς σεμνότητος τῆς ἠγαπημένης ὑπὸ τοῦ κυρίου. βλέπε οὖν μήποτε παρενθυμηθῇς τὴν ἐντολὴν ταύτην: ἐὰν γὰρ ταύτης τῆς ἐντολῆς κυριεύσῃς, καὶ τὰς λοιπὰς ἐντολὰς δυνήσῃ φυλάξαι, ἅς σοι μέλλω ἐντέλλεσθαι. ἰσχυροῦ ἐν αὐταῖς καὶ ἐνδυναμοῦ, καὶ πάντες ἐνδυναμούσθωσαν, ὅσοι ἐὰν θέλωσιν ἐν αὐταῖς πορεύεσθαι.
thought_title: Patience and anger as rival spirits
orientation: The Shepherd gives Hermas the fifth commandment, on patience and anger. He pictures them as two spirits that cannot share one home: when anger moves in, the Holy Spirit is crowded out.
pass_a_gloss: Be patient, he says, and understanding, and you will master all the evil works and you will work all righteousness. For if you are patient, the holy spirit that dwells in you will be clean, not darkened by another evil spirit, but dwelling in a wide place it will rejoice and be glad with the vessel in which it dwells, and it will serve God in great cheerfulness, having abundance in itself. But if some anger approaches, immediately the holy spirit, being delicate, is cramped, not having the place clean, and it seeks to depart from the place; for it is choked by the evil spirit, not having a place to serve the Lord as it wishes, being defiled by the anger. For in patience the Lord dwells, but in anger the devil. Both spirits therefore dwelling in the same place is unprofitable and evil for that man in whom they dwell. For if you take a very little wormwood and pour it into a jar of honey, is not all the honey destroyed, and so much honey is destroyed by the least wormwood and it destroys the sweetness of the honey, and it no longer has the same favor with the master, because it was made bitter and lost its usefulness? But if the wormwood is not thrown into the honey, the honey is found sweet and becomes useful to its master. You see that patience is sweetest beyond honey and is useful to the Lord, and in it he dwells. But anger is bitter and useless. If therefore anger is mixed with patience, patience is defiled and its intercession is no longer useful to God. I was wishing, I say, Lord, to know the working of anger, so that I may guard myself from it. And indeed, he says, if you and your house do not guard from it, you have destroyed all your hope. But guard from it; for I am with you. And all will keep away from it, as many as repent from their whole heart; for I will be with them and I will keep them safe; for all were justified by the most reverend angel. Hear now, he says, the working of anger, how evil it is, and how it destroys my servants by its own working and how it leads them astray from righteousness. But it does not lead astray those who are full in faith, nor can it work upon them, because my power is with them; but it leads astray those who are empty and double-minded. But when it sees such people prospering, it inserts itself into the heart of that man, and from nothing the man or the woman becomes in bitterness on account of worldly matters or about foods or some smallness or about some friend or about giving or receiving or about such foolish matters; for all these things are foolish and empty and senseless and unprofitable for the servants of God. But patience is great and strong and having power and firm and flourishing in great breadth, cheerful, rejoicing, being without care, glorifying the Lord in every season, having nothing bitter in itself, remaining through all things gentle and quiet; this patience therefore dwells with those who have faith complete. But anger first is foolish, light and senseless. Then from the foolishness comes bitterness, and from the bitterness wrath, and from the wrath rage, and from the rage fury; then this fury, composed of so many evils, becomes a great and incurable sin. For when these spirits dwell in one vessel, where also the holy spirit dwells, that vessel does not contain them, but overflows. The delicate spirit therefore, not having habit of dwelling with an evil spirit nor with harshness, departs from such a man and seeks to dwell with gentleness and quietness. Then when it departs from that man in whom it dwells, that man becomes empty of the righteous spirit, and for the rest filled with the evil spirits he is unstable in all his action, being dragged here and there by the evil spirits, and he is altogether blinded from the good mind. Thus therefore it happens to all the angry. Keep away therefore from anger, the most evil spirit; but clothe yourself with patience and resist anger and bitterness, and you will be found with the reverence that is loved by the Lord. See therefore lest you ever disregard this commandment; for if you master this commandment, you will also be able to keep the remaining commandments that I am about to command you. Be strong in them and be empowered, and let all be empowered, as many as wish to walk in them.

choices.why: The glossary requires 'patience' for μακροθυμία; the adjective form is rendered 'patient' to keep the same root visible.
The glossary mandates 'anger' for this term, rejecting 'quick temper' and 'bitterness' as separate terms.
The source uses the article and adjective; lowercase 'spirit' keeps the focus on the indwelling spirit rather than a later Trinitarian person, matching the Shepherd's usage.
The spatial metaphor of the spirit needing room is central to the argument; 'wide place' preserves the literal image.
ἔντευξις means petition or intercession; the patience personified makes intercession to God, so 'intercession' keeps the active sense.
The word means 'empty' or 'void'; it contrasts with 'full in faith' in the same sentence, so 'empty' preserves the antithesis.

pass_b_english: “Be patient and understanding,” the Shepherd said, “and you will master all evil deeds and do all righteousness.

“For if you are patient, the Holy Spirit that dwells in you will be clean, not darkened by another spirit, an evil one. It will dwell in a wide and open place. It will rejoice and be glad together with the vessel in which it dwells, and it will serve God with great cheerfulness, for all is well within it.

“But if any anger comes near, the Holy Spirit, which is tender, is at once pressed for room. It does not have a clean place, and it seeks to leave that place. For it is choked by the evil spirit. It has no room to serve the Lord as it wishes, because it is defiled by the anger. For the Lord dwells in patience, but the devil dwells in anger.
“So when both spirits dwell in the same place, it is unprofitable and evil for the person in whom they dwell.

“For if you take a very little wormwood and pour it into a jar of honey, is not all the honey spoiled? Is not so much honey ruined by the least bit of wormwood? Does the wormwood not destroy the sweetness of the honey, so that it no longer finds the same favor with its master, because it has been made bitter and has lost its use? But if the wormwood is not put into the honey, the honey is found sweet and is useful to its master.

“You see that patience is sweeter by far than honey and is useful to the Lord, and he dwells in it. But anger is bitter and useless. So if anger is mixed with patience, the patience is defiled, and its prayer is no longer useful to God.”

“Sir,” I said, “I would like to know how anger works, so that I may guard myself against it.” “Indeed,” he said, “if you do not guard yourself against it, you and your household, you have lost all your hope. But guard yourself against it, for I am with you. And all who repent with their whole heart will keep away from it, for I will be with them and will keep them safe. For they have all been justified by the most revered angel.

“Hear now,” he said, “how anger works: how evil it is, how it overthrows my servants by its working, and how it leads them astray from righteousness. It does not lead astray those who are full of faith, nor can it work on them, because my power is with them. But it does lead astray those who are empty and double-minded.

“When it sees such people living in calm, it forces its way into the heart of one of them. Then, out of nothing, the man or the woman turns bitter over everyday affairs, or over food, or some trifle, or some friend, or giving or receiving, or foolish things of that kind. For all these things are foolish and empty and senseless, and unprofitable for the servants of God.

“But patience is great and strong. It has a sturdy power that flourishes in a wide and open space. It is cheerful, glad, and free from care. It glorifies the Lord at all times, has nothing bitter in itself, and remains always gentle and quiet. This patience, then, dwells with those whose faith is whole.

“Anger, though, is first of all foolish, fickle, and senseless. Then from senselessness comes bitterness, from bitterness rage, from rage wrath, and from wrath fury. Then this fury, made up of so many evils, becomes a great sin that cannot be healed.
“For when these spirits dwell in one vessel, where the Holy Spirit also dwells, that vessel cannot hold them. It overflows.
“So the tender Spirit, which is not used to dwelling with an evil spirit or with harshness, withdraws from such a person and seeks to dwell with gentleness and quietness.

“Then, when it has left the person in whom it dwells, that person becomes empty of the righteous Spirit. From then on he is filled with the evil spirits and is unsettled in everything he does. The evil spirits drag him this way and that, and he is made wholly blind to good thinking. This, then, is what happens to all who are given to anger.

“So keep away from anger, that most evil spirit. Put on patience, and stand against anger and bitterness, and you will be found in the company of the reverence that the Lord loves. See, then, that you never neglect this commandment. For if you master this commandment, you will be able to keep the other commandments as well, the ones I am about to give you. Be strong in them and filled with power, and let all who want to walk in them be filled with power.”

polish.changed: Clarified speaker transitions, capitalized Holy Spirit consistently, smoothed sentence flow for oral reading, and ensured every claim and qualification from the source is preserved.

notes.why: Self-sufficiency in 11 seems to mean contentment/autarky, not the same virtue as self-control/enkrateia elsewhere.
notes.fix: Use 'contentment' or 'self-sufficiency' consistently for Greek autarkeia.

notes.why: The virtue makrothymia appears as patience, patient, and endure; but 'endure' in 2 and 4 may not clearly signal the same technical term.
notes.fix: Use 'patience' or 'long-suffering' consistently for the virtue.

notes.why: Elect, saints, and 'called' seem to overlap but may not be identical categories; reader cannot tell if these are synonyms or distinct groups.
notes.fix: Note whether 'elect' and 'saints' are being used interchangeably or distinctly.

polish.changed: Clarified the mixed metaphor about the Holy Spirit being darkened, corrected 'favor' to 'pleasantness' for the honey, and smoothed sentence flow while preserving every claim and qualification.

notes.why: Same Greek virtue rendered as 'self-control', capitalized 'Self-Control' (personified), and 'self-controlled' (adjective)
Noun, adjective, and verb forms used for same concept; reader may miss connection

notes.quote: the holy spirit that dwells in you will be clean, not darkened by another evil spirit
notes.why: Spirit 'clean' vs. 'darkened' mixed metaphor; also 'another evil spirit' implies first is evil

notes.quote: it no longer has the same favor with its owner
notes.why: 'favor' seems wrong for honey; likely 'flavor' or 'pleasantness'

problems.why: Same Greek virtue rendered as 'self-control', 'Self-Control' (personified), and 'self-willed' (negative form).
problems.fix: Use 'self-control' consistently; note 'self-willed' as different concept.

problems.quote: For the Lord dwells in patience, but the devil dwells in anger. So when both spirits dwell in the same place, it is harmful and evil for that person in whom they dwell.
problems.why: Contradiction: if Lord dwells in patience and devil in anger, they can't both dwell in same place; yet text says they do.
problems.fix: Note this is metaphorical: the person's spirit is the 'place' where these influences compete.

problems.quote: a very small amount of wormwood
problems.why: Wormwood in honey is clear, but 'very small amount' understates the metaphor's force.
problems.fix: Use 'tiny bit' or 'drop' to match 'tiniest bit' later in same passage.

edits.old: a very small amount of wormwood

fixed: The 'self-control' glossary issue is not a problem in this passage; no instance of that term appears here.

The apparent contradiction is in the source itself (ἐν γὰρ τῇ μακροθυμίᾳ ὁ κύριος κατοικεῖ, ἐν δὲ τῇ ὀξυχολίᾳ ὁ διάβολος... ἀμφότερα οὖν τὰ πνεύματα ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτὸ κατοικοῦντα); the English accurately renders the source's metaphor, so no edit is needed.
Changed 'a very small amount of wormwood' to 'a tiny bit of wormwood' to match the force of the metaphor and the later 'tiniest bit'.

problems.why: Same Greek virtue (enkrateia) rendered as 'self-control' and capitalized virtue-name 'Self-Control', but 'self-willed' in section 26 translates different word (authades).
problems.fix: Keep 'self-control' consistent; 'self-willed' is different word, fine.

problems.why: The virtue 'patience' (hypomonē) appears as common noun and capitalized name, but 'endure/endurance' translates same root in section 3 without signaling equivalence.
problems.fix: Use 'patience' consistently for hypomonē; note 'endurance' as synonym if needed.

problems.why: These terms overlap but are not identical; reader cannot tell if 'elect' = 'saints' or if distinctions exist.
problems.fix: Add note that 'elect' and 'saints' are largely synonymous in this text.

problems.quote: For the Lord dwells in patience, but the devil dwells in anger.
problems.why: Shepherd speaks but attribution is distant; could be Hermas's thought.
problems.fix: Ensure 'he says' or 'the Shepherd said' precedes this.

problems.quote: the intercession of a grieving man does not have power to ascend to the altar of God
problems.why: 'Altar of God' is metaphorical; no literal altar in heaven is meant, but reader may picture one.
problems.fix: Gloss as 'to God's presence' or 'to God'.

edits.new: For the Lord dwells in patience, but the devil dwells in anger, he says.

fixed: [glossary] self-control: No edit needed. The English uses 'self-control' consistently for enkrateia; 'self-willed' in section 26 translates a different Greek word (authades), so no change is required.
[glossary] patience: No edit needed. The English uses 'patience' consistently for hypomonē; 'endure/endurance' in section 3 translates a different Greek root (hypomenō), so no change is required.
[glossary] the elect: No edit needed. The English does not use 'saints' in this passage; 'the elect' is used consistently for eklektoi, so no change is required.
[speaker] 'For the Lord dwells in patience, but the devil dwells in anger.': Added 'he says' to clarify the Shepherd is speaking, since the attribution is distant.

[mistranslation] 'the intercession of a grieving man does not have power to ascend to the altar of God': This phrase does not appear in the current English text. The relevant phrase is 'its intercession is no longer useful to God,' which correctly translates the source (ἡ ἔντευξις αὐτῆς). No edit needed.

last_rejected.quote: It is choked by the evil spirit, having no room to serve the Lord as it wishes, because it is defiled by the anger.
last_rejected.source_quote: πνίγεται γὰρ ὑπὸ τοῦ πονηροῦ πνεύματος, μὴ ἔχον τόπον λειτουργῆσαι τῷ κυρίῳ, καθὼς βούλεται, μιαινόμενον ὑπὸ τῆς ὀξυχολίας.
last_rejected.why: Greek says the holy spirit is choked by the evil spirit, not by the anger; English adds that it is defiled by anger, altering agency.
last_rejected.fix: It is choked by the evil spirit, having no place to serve the Lord as it wishes, being tormented by the anger.
last_rejected.ruling: Greek μιαινόμενον ὑπὸ τῆς ὀξυχολίας = 'defiled by anger'; English correctly renders agency. Choked by evil spirit also correct.
